thesis: Your implementation capacity can cap your software growth.

picks.title: How Much Services Revenue Can You Live With?
picks.author: CJ Gustafson
picks.why: A finance-side case for handing repeatable implementation work to partners: the reason is capacity more than margin, and the cost is a few quarters of uglier revenue. It gives you the numbers to explain a partner-delivery shift to people who own the plan. Caveats: the worked example is illustrative, the rule of thumb comes from one vertical software CFO, and reading time is estimated from about 1,800 words of essay.
lookFor: Why does the CFO worry more about implementation capacity than about services margin?
Which implementations should stay with your own team, and when should a type of deployment move to partners?
What has to be agreed with owners before the shift, so the plan does not count the drop in services revenue as a miss?
picks.gist: Services revenue carries maybe 20-30% gross margin and gets no software multiple, but it is often what lets customers go live, so cutting it blindly can choke subscription growth. The CFO quoted aims for services under 20% of revenue and growing slower than software, keeps the first deployments of new modules in-house to learn where they break, and lets systems integrators lead the rest, reporting the number of certified outside consultants as real capacity. In the worked example, moving 8 of 15 in services to partners makes total revenue fall 5% in year one while gross profit rises, and only in year two do revenue and gross profit both clearly exceed the start. The practical advice: split services into work only you can do versus repeatable work, measure how far out the implementation team is booked, and count certified people outside the company, not partner logos.

picks.title: Token Series Part 3 | Who’s Footing the Bill for AI?
picks.author: CJ Gustafson with Ali Hussain
picks.domain: Pricing, packaging and activation in a self-serve funnel
picks.why: A short conversation on who pays for AI usage once the venture subsidy fades, and how pricing is moving to hybrid commits, tiers and credits with overages. Useful if you package AI features into a self-serve plan. Caveats: the guest runs a billing software company that sponsors the series, so treat his view of overages and revenue leakage as interested; the summary comes from the show notes and chapter list. A search today found hybrid base-plus-credits pricing still described as the common model, so nothing contradicts it yet.
lookFor: When does passing token costs to the customer make sense, and when will a buyer switch to a cheaper tool?
What problem does a credit solve that a plain per-unit price does not, and what does it hide from the buyer?
How do they suggest handling overages without surprising the customer?
picks.gist: The episode starts from the point that today's AI prices are partly subsidised by venture money, sizes AI spend and compares it to early ride-hailing prices. It then covers companies passing token costs through to customers and whether buyers will move to cheaper options. The middle part is on packaging: hybrid commitments, where tiers fit and what a credit is. It closes on the overage problem, revenue leakage and agent-driven buying, and sets up a next part on tokens as a currency.

practice.title: What moving services to partners does to the numbers
practice.prompt: Pen and paper, no calculator. Your company has 60 in revenue: 45 subscription at 85% gross margin and 15 services at 25%. Step 1 (3 min): compute gross profit, blended gross margin and services share today. Step 2 (4 min): in year one you hand 8 of services to partners and subscription grows by 5. Compute revenue, its change in percent, gross profit, blended margin and services share. Then say how much gross profit you gave up and how much you gained. Step 3 (5 min): each new customer needs 400 implementation hours and one consultant delivers about 1,200 billable hours a year. Sales wants 60 new customers next year and you have 12 consultants. How many customers can your own team take live, and how many certified outside consultants do you need for the rest?
practice.reveal: Step 1: 45 x 0.85 = 38.25 and 15 x 0.25 = 3.75, so gross profit is 42, blended margin 42 / 60 = 70%, services share 15 / 60 = 25%. Step 2: subscription 50, services 7, revenue 57, a 5% drop. Gross profit 50 x 0.85 = 42.5 plus 7 x 0.25 = 1.75, so 44.25; blended margin 44.25 / 57 is about 77.6%; services share 7 / 57 is about 12%. You gave up 8 x 0.25 = 2 of gross profit and gained 5 x 0.85 = 4.25, net +2.25, which matches 44.25 - 42. Revenue fell while gross profit rose, which is the story you have to tell in advance. Step 3: 12 consultants x 1,200 hours = 14,400 hours, enough for 14,400 / 400 = 36 customers. The other 24 customers need 24 x 400 = 9,600 hours, so 8 full-time outside consultants, and more in practice, since partners will not give you all of their hours. Without them, adding salespeople past 36 new customers only lengthens the queue to go live.
